title: Nice, not needed
hookLine: Stoics prefer health and wealth but don't stake their happiness on them

lines: SO A STOIC SHRUGS AT A BROKEN LEG?
cards: Two days ago the Stoics said health and money aren't truly good. Easy to say from a marble bench. So does a Stoic shrug at a broken leg?
Turn down a raise? Live on cold water and gravel? No.
The reason is a careful piece of sorting: the difference between something you'd like and something you need. A warm coat on a cold day. A good night's sleep.
A full fridge. Nice. Very nice.

teach.b: Adiaphora is Greek for indifferents, things that don't make a difference. Not to your comfort; there they make a big difference. They make no difference to whether you're a good person.
Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself: all indifferent in that one sense. But the Stoics sorted the indifferents.

Some are preferred: health over sickness, enough money over poverty, friends over loneliness. It's natural and sensible to pick those, and a Stoic will. Others are dispreferred, and it's sensible to avoid them.
Zeno explained the word preferred with a picture from a royal court, which Cicero passes on.

teach.h: NEAR THE THRONE, NEVER THE KING.
teach.b: At court, the ministers and nobles are promoted, placed near the throne. But none of them is the king. Health and money are like that: high in rank, never the ruler.

Only character sits on the throne. Seneca was a very rich man, and in his essay On the Happy Life he answers critics who threw that at him. Roughly: the wise person may own wealth, but wealth must not own him.
Epictetus gives the gentlest picture of all, in his Handbook: behave in life as at a banquet.

teach.h: TAKE A SHARE AT THE BANQUET.
teach.b: When a dish comes around to you, reach out and take a polite share.
If it passes you by, don't grab at it. If it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch across the table. Enjoy what's in front of you.
Just don't stake your happiness on the next plate.

how: Stoic practitioners enjoy comforts and pursue sensible goals like health and income, while reminding themselves that these are preferred, not necessary for a good life.

o: small sins that don't really count as wrong
pleasures a wise person should always refuse
things like health: nice to have, not truly good

p: things that don't make you good or bad
near the throne, never the king

s: Stoics turn down comfort and health
health and wealth are preferred; a Stoic sensibly picks them.
Zeno compared preferred things to nobles at a royal court
high in rank, but never the king. Only character rules.
he was very rich, and in On the Happy Life he answers critics who pointed it out.

games.q: you're at Epictetus's banquet. a dish you love passes you by. what does he advise?
games.why: take a polite share when it comes, don't grab when it passes, don't stretch for what hasn't arrived.

practice: Choose one comfort that's with you right now, the chair under you, a warm drink, the quiet in the room, and enjoy it fully for a few breaths.
Then gently imagine it gone: the chair harder, the drink cold, the room loud; you'd still be you. Come back to the comfort, and hold it a little more lightly.

wordCard.voice: Adiaphora. Greek for indifferents: things like health and wealth that are worth preferring but don't make you good or bad. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: indifferents, things that don't make a difference to your character.

carryVoice: Your line: take a polite share. Near the throne, never the king. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
